questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon. Staging CT shows multiple new nodules in the liver, and biopsy of one confirms metastatic colonic adenocarcinoma. Which factor best explains why the liver was the site of these metastases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arterial spread of tumor cells through the hepatic artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemokine receptors that home tumor cells to hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic flow from the colon into hepatic lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across the peritoneal cavity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venous drainage of the colon passing first to the liver

explanation.summary: Colon cancer typically metastasizes to the liver because the liver is the first downstream organ of the colon's portal venous drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: One key factor determining where circulating tumor cells end up is the location and vascular drainage of the primary tumor. All portal blood from the colon drains into the liver, so tumor cells lodge in the first capillary bed they reach there; the lecture gives colon-to-liver spread as the example of this anatomic factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterial spread is the less common hematogenous route because arterial walls are thick and elastin-rich.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemokine-receptor tropism is a separate factor; the lecture attributes colon-to-liver spread to vascular drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver is reached through portal venous blood, not through lymphatic drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding produces surface implants in the cavity (as with ovarian carcinoma), not drainage-based liver deposits.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is found to have a solid renal mass on imaging, and biopsy shows renal cell carcinoma. Unlike the usual pattern for tumors of epithelial origin, this tumor is classically known for which pattern of spread?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across the pleural cavity

explanation.summary: Renal cell carcinoma is one of four carcinomas known for hematogenous rather than lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most carcinomas spread lymphatically, but four are known for spreading hematogenously: follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread is the typical carcinoma route, which renal cell carcinoma is a notable exception to.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peritoneal seeding is the classic pattern of ovarian carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pleural seeding is a seeding route, not the characteristic route of renal cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is the pattern of glioblastoma within the brain and spinal cord.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has an enlarging deep mass in the thigh. Biopsy shows a malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin. By which route is this type of tumor most typically associated with spreading?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding across an adjacent joint cavity

explanation.summary: Sarcomas (mesenchymal tumors) are associated with hematogenous spread; carcinomas with lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcomas are of mesenchymal origin and are associated with hematogenous spread, whereas epithelial carcinomas are associated with lymphatic spread. This is a tendency rather than a fixed rule, but it is the typical association.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spread along epithelial surfaces is not one of the three main metastatic pathways described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread is the pattern associated with carcinomas, not sarcomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Joint cavities are among the open spaces where seeding can occur, but seeding is not the typical sarcoma route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peritoneal seeding is classic for ovarian carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman undergoes lumpectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma. Sections show tumor aggregates inside dilated lymphatic channels at the tumor edge and within a regional lymph node, but no tumor within blood vessels. Which property of lymphatic vessels best explains why carcinoma cells commonly enter them rather than blood vessels?

choices.label: B
choices.text: They carry rapid, high-shear flow that pulls cells in

choices.label: C
choices.text: They drain directly into the portal venous system

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have thick walls with abundant elastin

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack tight junctions and a basement membrane

explanation.summary: Lymphatic intravasation is mostly mechanical: lymphatics are low-shear and lack the tight junctions and basement membrane of blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lymphatic pathway is a low-shear system that does not have the tight junctions and basement membrane associated with blood vessels, making it easier for a tumor cell to get into a lymphatic vessel than into a blood vessel. This mechanical ease is why carcinomas such as breast cancer typically spread lymphatically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Laminin receptors are overexpressed by cancer cells, not by lymphatic endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatics are a low-shear system; shear stress kills circulating tumor cells rather than helping them enter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal venous drainage explains liver metastasis from the colon, stomach and pancreas, not lymphatic entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thick elastin-rich walls describe arteries and make them harder, not easier, to penetrate.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has progressive abdominal distension. At surgery, an ovarian carcinoma is found, along with numerous tumor nodules studding the omentum and the surfaces of the abdominal organs. By which mechanism did this tumor most likely reach these sites?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread through the portal vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across a body cavity

explanation.summary: Ovarian carcinoma is known for seeding the peritoneal cavity, including the omentum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding requires an open space such as the peritoneal cavity, pleural cavity, subarachnoid space or joint cavities, in which tumor cells are sown much as a gardener sows seeds. Ovarian carcinoma is the lecture's example of seeding the peritoneal cavity, with omental involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterial spread is uncommon and would not produce diffuse surface implants within a cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Portal venous spread delivers tumor to the liver parenchyma, not to omental and serosal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread produces nodal metastases, not implants across the peritoneal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is how glioblastoma spreads within the brain and spinal cord.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a malignancy begins a chemotherapy regimen that includes methotrexate. Which molecular target does this drug directly inhibit to interfere with DNA synthesis?

explanation.summary: Methotrexate, an S-phase antimetabolite, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and blocks formation of reduced folates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methotrexate binds to and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, inhibiting the formation of reduced folates, and thymidylate synthetase, resulting in inhibition of purine and thymidylic acid synthesis. This interferes with DNA synthesis, repair and cellular replication in the S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD20 on B cells is the target of rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase inhibition is the primary action of cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The topoisomerase I-DNA complex is the target of irinotecan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tubulin is the target of the microtubule inhibitors (vinca alkaloids and taxanes).

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is started on a taxane. Her oncologist explains that, although this drug and the vinca alkaloids both act on microtubules during mitosis, their effects on microtubules differ. Which mechanism characterizes the taxane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds tubulin and blocks formation of new microtubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-links DNA strands regardless of cycle phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits DNA polymerase after DNA incorporation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stabilizes microtubules and blocks their disassembly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traps topoisomerase I and blocks DNA religation

explanation.summary: Taxanes promote and stabilize microtubules and prevent their disassembly; vinca alkaloids block microtubule formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taxanes promote microtubule assembly by enhancing the action of tubulin dimers, stabilizing existing microtubules and inhibiting their disassembly, which interferes with mitosis. The vinca alkaloids do the opposite at the same target: they bind tubulin and inhibit microtubule formation, arresting cells at metaphase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking microtubule formation describes the vinca alkaloids, the contrast drug in the stem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phase-independent DNA cross-linking describes the alkylating and platinum agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase inhibition after incorporation into DNA describes cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trapping topoisomerase I and blocking religation describes irinotecan.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with bladder cancer is treated with cisplatin. Which pairing correctly describes this drug's mechanism and its relationship to the cell cycle?

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA strand breakage; specific to G2 phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate antagonism; specific to S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spindle disruption; specific to M phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase I block; specific to S phase

explanation.summary: Platinum agents, like alkylating agents, cross-link DNA chains and act independently of the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alkylating agents operate independently of the cell cycle, cross-linking DNA chains and causing them to break, which inhibits DNA replication and transcription. The same mechanism is observed in the platinum agents carboplatin and cisplatin, used in cancers including bladder cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA strand breakage in G2 phase describes bleomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate antagonism in S phase describes methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spindle disruption in M phase describes the microtubule inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase I inhibition describes irinotecan.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has invasive breast carcinoma. Testing shows the tumor is estrogen receptor-negative and strongly HER2-positive. Which agent directly targets the receptor that is overexpressed by her tumor?

explanation.summary: Trastuzumab binds HER2 receptors and is primarily used for HER2-positive breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trastuzumab binds to HER2 receptors on tumor cells, blocking the signaling pathways that drive growth and marking the cells for immune-mediated destruction. It is primarily used for HER2-positive breast cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis rather than a receptor on the tumor cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CAR-T cells are a cell therapy, not an agent described as targeting HER2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and is used for B-cell malignancies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tamoxifen is a SERM used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer; this tumor is ER-negative.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy for lung cancer develops persistent nausea and vomiting, and a routine blood count shows marked decreases in all cell lines. His sister, treated with a monoclonal antibody for a different cancer, had far fewer adverse effects. Which feature of his drugs best accounts for both of his adverse effects?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of tumor angiogenesis through VEGF

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preferential injury to cells resting in G0

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective binding to tumor surface receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells

explanation.summary: Most cytotoxic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, so gastric mucosa (nausea/vomiting) and bone marrow (myelosuppression) are injured.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because most chemotherapeutic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, not just cancer cells, they also kill normal cells that turn over rapidly. Drugs affecting gastric mucosa lead to nausea and vomiting, and drugs affecting bone marrow cause myelosuppression. More specific agents such as monoclonal antibodies act in a targeted way, reducing the number and intensity of adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune checkpoints are pathways tumors use to turn off immunity; cytotoxic drugs do not act by activating them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VEGF blockade is the mechanism of bevacizumab, not of cytotoxic chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells in G0 are nondividing; cytotoxic toxicity falls on rapidly cycling cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective receptor binding is the property of targeted monoclonal antibodies and explains their milder toxicity.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with a mass in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. Mammography shows a nodule in that region, and core needle biopsy demonstrates invasive ductal carcinoma. At surgery a sentinel lymph node biopsy is planned. Based on the location of this tumor, which group of lymph nodes is most likely to be involved first?

explanation.summary: Lymph node involvement follows the path of lymphatic drainage from the primary tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breast cancers arising in the upper outer quadrant drain first to the nearby axillary lymph nodes because of the anatomy of lymphatic drainage. These are therefore the sentinel and most likely first-involved nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Infraclavicular nodes are more distal and would typically be involved only later in the sequence of spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mediastinal (internal mammary) nodes are associated with drainage from the inner quadrants of the breast, not the upper outer quadrant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Submandibular nodes drain the head and neck and are rarely involved in breast cancer spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supraclavicular nodes are distal nodes that become involved later in metastatic progression.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman noticed a mole enlarging over the past several years. A dermatologist performs a biopsy that shows melanoma, and a sentinel lymph node biopsy reveals metastatic disease. Inactivation of which normal cell structure most directly permits tumor cells to detach from one another and begin invasion?

explanation.summary: Loss of E-cadherin frees tumor cells from one another, an early step in invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: E-cadherin connects epithelial cells to one another; its inactivation leads to loss of intercellular adhesion, one of the first steps of invasion. Loss of E-cadherin classically produces the single-file infiltration pattern of invasive lobular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Actin filaments drive migration of the tumor cell through the extracellular matrix rather than mediating cell-cell adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoplakin is part of the normal cell structure but does not itself trigger the invasion of tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gap junctions mediate cell-to-cell communication; their inactivation would not lead to invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Keratin is an important structural component, but loss of keratin does not result in invasion.

questions.stem: A researcher is describing the metastatic cascade to a class of students. She defines one step as the tumor cell breaching the basement membrane, migrating through the extracellular matrix, and entering a vessel. Which step of metastasis is she describing?

explanation.summary: Intravasation is tumor cell invasion through the ECM and entry into a vessel.
explanation.whyCorrect: The steps of metastasis are invasion, intravasation, extravasation, and growth at secondary sites. Intravasation corresponds to tumor cell invasion through the extracellular matrix and entry into the bloodstream or lymphatics to travel toward a secondary site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiogenesis is new vessel formation and is not the step of entering a vessel described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colonization is the later outgrowth at a distant organ, which depends on a favorable stromal environment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extravasation is the opposite directional step: tumor cells exit the bloodstream or lymphatics and infiltrate outside the capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor dormancy refers to failure to grow at a distant site, not entry into a vessel.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with colon adenocarcinoma undergoes staging imaging that reveals multiple hepatic lesions consistent with metastases. Which feature best explains why the liver is the most common initial site of metastasis for colon cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon cancer cells preferentially spread through the lymphatics to the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Portal venous blood from the colon drains into the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seeding across the peritoneal cavity deposits cells directly onto the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: The liver has an unusually high oxygen content that favors tumor growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver secretes chemokines that specifically attract colonic tumor cells

explanation.summary: Hematogenous spread often follows normal venous drainage to the first capillary bed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hematogenous spread, tumor cells follow the normal venous drainage pattern and embed in the first capillary bed they reach. All portal blood from the colon, stomach, and pancreas drains into the liver, which is why the liver is a common first site of metastasis for these cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The described colon-to-liver pattern is hematogenous through the portal vein, not lymphatic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seeding requires an open cavity and does not describe the venous drainage responsible for hepatic metastasis here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arteries carry higher oxygen content, but this makes arterial spread less common; it does not explain hepatic metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While tropism and chemokine receptors influence some metastases, the brick attributes colon-to-liver spread to anatomic vascular drainage, not liver-secreted chemokines.

questions.stem: A pathologist notes that although most carcinomas spread through the lymphatics, a small group of carcinomas is classically known for spreading hematogenously. Which of the following carcinomas belongs to that group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonic adenocarcinoma spreading to regional nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: Four carcinomas are classically known for hematogenous spread: follicular thyroid, choriocarcinoma, renal cell, and hepatocellular.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most carcinomas spread lymphatically, four are known for hematogenous spread: follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Renal cell carcinoma is a member of this group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Regional nodal spread of colon cancer is lymphatic; it is not part of the classic hematogenous carcinoma group.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is not among the four carcinomas singled out for hematogenous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast carcinoma is the brick's classic example of lymphatic (axillary node) spread, not the hematogenous exception group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Squamous cell carcinoma is a carcinoma that follows the usual lymphatic route and is not in the four-carcinoma hematogenous group.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is diagnosed with osteosarcoma of the distal femur. When counseling about the most likely route by which this tumor will disseminate, which pattern of spread should be emphasized?

explanation.summary: Sarcomas, being of mesenchymal origin, are associated with hematogenous spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcomas are of mesenchymal origin and are associated with hematogenous spread through the bloodstream, in contrast to carcinomas, which are associated with lymphatic spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Perineural spread is not the route emphasized for sarcomas in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread is the pattern classically associated with carcinomas (epithelial-derived tumors), not sarcomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding requires shedding into an open cavity, as with ovarian carcinoma, and is not the typical route for a bone sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is characteristic of CNS tumors such as glioblastoma, not osteosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with high-grade ovarian carcinoma is found at laparotomy to have numerous tumor nodules studding the omentum and peritoneal surfaces, without an intervening path through lymphatics or blood vessels. Which mechanism of tumor spread best accounts for this distribution?

explanation.summary: Seeding disseminates tumor across an open body cavity such as the peritoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding requires an open space such as the peritoneal, pleural, subarachnoid, or joint cavities. Ovarian carcinoma is a classic example of a tumor that seeds the peritoneal cavity, producing widespread surface implants such as omental involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematogenous spread deposits cells in capillary beds of organs, not as surface seeding across a cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread travels through lymphatic channels to nodes and would not produce diffuse peritoneal surface implants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perineural invasion is spread along nerves and does not explain diffuse peritoneal implants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor dormancy describes failure to grow at a distant site, not the mechanism producing peritoneal implants.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with glioblastoma develops new neurologic deficits, and imaging reveals tumor deposits within the spinal subarachnoid space. Which route of spread best explains dissemination of this tumor from the brain to the spinal cord?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread through the vertebral veins

explanation.summary: Glioblastomas use the open subarachnoid space to seed the brain and spinal cord.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding occurs within open spaces, and glioblastomas use the subarachnoid space to seed within the brain and spinal cord. The cerebrospinal fluid within this open space carries cells to distant CNS surfaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct extension through bone does not explain deposits floating within the subarachnoid space.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes CNS glioblastoma dissemination to seeding through the subarachnoid space rather than hematogenous venous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The CNS lacks conventional lymphatics used for this spread, and the brick describes seeding, not lymphatic dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retrograde perineural spread is not the mechanism the brick describes for glioblastoma.

questions.stem: In an experiment, tumor cells are engineered to overexpress a receptor that binds a major component of the basement membrane, which markedly increases their adhesion to basement membranes and their ability to invade surrounding tissues and blood vessels. Overexpression of a receptor for which molecule best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Laminin receptor overexpression promotes tumor adhesion to and invasion through basement membranes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can overexpress laminin receptors. These receptors bind laminin, a major component of the basement membrane, facilitating tumor cell adhesion to basement membranes, migration, and invasion into surrounding tissues and blood vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin is a plasma transport protein and is not a basement membrane component mediating invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoplakin is part of desmosomes and does not serve as the basement membrane ligand described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin is an intracellular oxygen carrier in red blood cells and is unrelated to basement membrane adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratin is an intracellular structural protein of epithelial cells, not a basement membrane ligand for an invasion-promoting receptor.

questions.stem: During intravasation, most single circulating tumor cells die, yet some survive to establish distant metastases. According to the theory described, which behavior most improves a circulating tumor cell's chance of survival in the bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Downregulating all surface adhesion molecules to travel as single cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shrinking below the diameter of a red blood cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traveling as multicellular aggregates bound to platelets

explanation.summary: Tumor cells that clump and bind platelets survive circulation better than lone cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: A theory of which tumor cells ultimately metastasize holds that circulating cells are much more likely to migrate as multicellular aggregates than as single cells. Tumor cells bind to one another or to platelets to survive in the bloodstream and may activate coagulation factors, forming emboli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of adhesion promotes apoptosis, and single cells are far more likely to die than aggregates, so this reduces survival.
whyWrongByChoice.B: High shear stress from flow kills circulating tumor cells rather than protecting them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tumor cells are significantly larger than most blood cells; they do not shrink below a red blood cell, and their size helps them lodge in capillary beds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor cells tend to activate coagulation factors to form protective emboli, so suppressing coagulation would not aid survival.

questions.stem: A student asks why tumor cells more readily enter lymphatic vessels than blood vessels during metastasis. Which property of the lymphatic system best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It actively secretes proteases that pull tumor cells inward

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carries a higher oxygen content that attracts tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directs all cells immediately to the liver and lungs

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has thicker, muscular walls that trap tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lacks the tight junctions and basement membrane of blood vessels

explanation.summary: Lymphatics are a low-shear, loosely walled system that tumor cells enter easily.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reason a tumor cell intravasates lymphatically is largely mechanical. The lymphatic pathway is a low-shear system that lacks the tight junctions and basement membrane associated with blood vessels, making it easier for a tumor cell to enter a lymphatic vessel than a blood vessel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphatics do not actively secrete proteases to pull in tumor cells; proteases come from tumor cells and nearby stromal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Higher oxygen content describes arterial blood; it is not a feature that draws tumor cells into lymphatics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drainage to the liver and lungs reflects venous/portal hematogenous patterns, not lymphatic entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphatic vessels are thin-walled and low-shear, not thick and muscular; that is a feature of arteries.

questions.stem: To avoid the morbidity of a full axillary dissection, a breast surgeon injects tracer around a tumor and removes the first node that takes up the tracer to assess for metastasis. Which statement best describes the node being sampled?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a node that filters hematogenously spread tumor emboli

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the contralateral supraclavicular node

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the first node in a regional lymphatic basin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the first node the surgeon encounters on entering the axilla

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the most distal node in the lymphatic chain draining the tumor

explanation.summary: The sentinel node is the first node in a regional basin receiving lymph from the tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: In breast cancer, axillary lymph node assessment guides prognosis and therapy. To avoid the morbidity of a full dissection, the surgeon biopsies the sentinel lymph node, defined as the first node in a regional lymphatic basin that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor and is thus the likely first site of spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sentinel node concept is based on lymphatic drainage, not on filtering hematogenous tumor emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A contralateral supraclavicular node is not the first regional draining node and is not the sentinel node of an axillary basin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sentinel node is defined by tracer uptake and lymphatic drainage, not by which node the surgeon happens to encounter first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sentinel node is the first, most proximal node receiving drainage, not the most distal node in the chain.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukemia begins an induction regimen that includes a folate antagonist. The drug reduces the pool of reduced folates, thereby impairing purine and thymidylic acid synthesis and blocking progression of cells from G1 into S phase. Which of the following enzymes does this agent most directly inhibit?

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is an S-phase antimetabolite that blocks folate metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methotrexate binds and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (and thymidylate synthetase), preventing formation of reduced folates. This blocks purine and thymidylic acid synthesis, interfering with DNA synthesis, repair, and replication and preventing the G1-to-S transition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of DNA polymerase is the primary action of the pyrimidine analog cytarabine, not methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topoisomerase I is the target of irinotecan, which prevents relegation of cleaved DNA strands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase is an antiviral target and is unrelated to cytotoxic chemotherapy mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interference with tubulin/microtubule dynamics describes vinca alkaloids and taxanes, not a folate antagonist.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia has been receiving induction chemotherapy that includes vincristine. Several weeks into treatment he develops difficulty walking, frequent tripping, and tingling and numbness of his fingers and toes. Examination shows decreased deep tendon reflexes, mild foot drop, and reduced grip strength. Which of the following adverse effects best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Vinca alkaloids characteristically cause peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vincristine inhibits microtubule formation and affects rapidly turning-over and nerve cells, producing peripheral neuropathy. Tingling, numbness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and foot drop are classic; caught early, it can be managed with dose reduction and monitoring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiotoxicity is the signature toxicity of doxorubicin (anthracyclines), not vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is associated with cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary fibrosis is characteristic of bleomycin and busulfan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nephrotoxicity is a hallmark toxicity of the platinum agents cisplatin and carboplatin.

questions.stem: A researcher studies why some cancer cells continue to divide despite carrying extensive DNA damage. In normal cells, a series of surveillance points halts progression when DNA is damaged or the environment is unfavorable. Which of the following best describes the normal function of these cell cycle checkpoints?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They accelerate division of cells with damaged DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: They halt division and trigger apoptosis in damaged cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: They mark tumor cells for destruction by monoclonal antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: They replicate chromosomal DNA during S phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: They synthesize the microtubules of the mitotic spindle

explanation.summary: Checkpoints arrest the cycle and drive apoptosis of cells with damaged DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The G1/S, G2/M, and metaphase/anaphase checkpoints ensure a cell is ready to divide. DNA damage or an unfavorable environment halts the cycle and drives apoptosis, eliminating 'bad' cells. In cancer these checkpoints are often broken, permitting uncontrolled division.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Checkpoints restrain, not accelerate, division of damaged cells; loss of this restraint is what characterizes cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marking tumor cells for immune destruction describes monoclonal antibodies, not intrinsic checkpoints.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA replication is the defining event of S phase, not the function of a checkpoint.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microtubule synthesis occurs in G2 phase and is not the role of a checkpoint.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops progressive dyspnea and fatigue. Echocardiography shows a decline in left ventricular ejection fraction. Which of the following chemotherapeutic agents is most likely responsible for this toxicity?

explanation.summary: Doxorubicin (an anthracycline) is the classic cause of cardiotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline that cross-links DNA independently of the cell cycle, is characteristically associated with cardiotoxicity, which can manifest as declining ejection fraction and heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine is associated with keratitis and conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is associated with severe acute and delayed diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression, not cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is associated with peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man being treated for lymphoma develops dysuria and gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows diffuse bladder mucosal inflammation and bleeding. Which of the following chemotherapeutic agents most likely caused this finding?

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide characteristically causes hemorrhagic cystitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent whose signature toxicity is hemorrhagic cystitis, presenting with dysuria and hematuria from bladder mucosal injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin is associated with pulmonary fibrosis, not bladder toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity rather than hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man treated for testicular cancer develops a gradually worsening dry cough and dyspnea. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity, and imaging suggests interstitial fibrosis. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Bleomycin is the classic cause of pulmonary fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleomycin, a G2-phase agent that binds DNA and causes strand breaks, characteristically produces pulmonary fibrosis, presenting as progressive dyspnea and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytarabine causes keratitis and conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is associated with severe diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy develops a rising serum creatinine and new bilateral high-frequency hearing loss confirmed on audiometry. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for both findings?

explanation.summary: Platinum agents such as cisplatin cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cisplatin is a platinum agent that cross-links DNA independently of the cell cycle; its signature toxicities include both nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, explaining the rising creatinine and hearing loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclophosphamide characteristically causes hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is started on a monoclonal antibody that binds an antigen on the surface of B cells, rendering them more susceptible to destruction by the immune system. Which of the following is the target of this agent?

explanation.summary: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rituximab acts on CD20 receptors on B cells, making them more susceptible to immune-mediated attack. It is used for B-cell malignancies such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HER2 is the target of trastuzumab, used in HER2-positive breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topoisomerase I is inhibited by irinotecan, a cytotoxic agent rather than an antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tubulin is targeted by microtubule inhibitors (vinca alkaloids, taxanes), not a monoclonal antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF is bound by bevacizumab to inhibit angiogenesis.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic colorectal cancer receives a monoclonal antibody intended to cut off the tumor's blood supply. The drug binds a circulating protein that drives the abnormal blood vessel proliferation supporting the tumor. Which of the following is the molecular target of this agent?

choices.label: C
choices.text: HER2 receptor on tumor cell membranes

explanation.summary: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bevacizumab binds vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), inhibiting the angiogenesis that accompanies tumor growth. Without a vascular supply, the cancer cells die.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD20 is the target of rituximab on B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The CD3 receptor is the T-cell component onto which CAR-T constructs are fused, not a bevacizumab target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HER2 is the target of trastuzumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, a cytotoxic antimetabolite.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a breast tumor that overexpresses HER2. Her oncologist recommends a monoclonal antibody that binds this receptor to block downstream growth signaling and mark the cells for immune-mediated destruction. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Trastuzumab targets HER2-positive breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trastuzumab binds HER2 receptors on tumor cells, blocking the signaling pathways that drive growth and marking the cells for immune-mediated destruction. It is used primarily for HER2-positive breast cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis, not the HER2 receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxorubicin is a cytotoxic anthracycline that cross-links DNA, not a HER2-directed antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells for B-cell malignancies, not HER2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, a different target.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is treated with irinotecan. The agent and its active metabolite bind reversibly to a DNA-associated enzyme, preventing relegation of the cleaved DNA strand and producing double-strand breaks during S phase. Which of the following enzymes does this agent inhibit?

explanation.summary: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irinotecan and its active metabolite bind reversibly to the topoisomerase I-DNA complex, preventing relegation of the cleaved strand. This produces double-strand breaks that cells cannot efficiently repair, causing S-phase-specific cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase is the primary target of cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymidylate synthetase is inhibited by methotrexate, not irinotecan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tubulin is bound by microtubule inhibitors such as the vinca alkaloids and taxanes.

questions.stem: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia receives cytarabine. This agent is incorporated into DNA, but its primary action is inhibition of an enzyme required for DNA synthesis and repair, and it is specific for the S phase. Which of the following best describes cytarabine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody directed against CD20

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: A taxane that stabilizes microtubules and blocks disassembly

choices.label: D
choices.text: A vinca alkaloid that binds tubulin and arrests metaphase

choices.label: E
choices.text: An alkylating agent that cross-links DNA independently of the cycle

explanation.summary: Cytarabine is an S-phase pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytarabine is a pyrimidine analog incorporated into DNA, but its primary action is inhibition of DNA polymerase, resulting in decreased DNA synthesis and repair. It is an S-phase-specific antimetabolite.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CD20-directed monoclonal antibody describes rituximab, not a cytotoxic antimetabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stabilizing microtubules and blocking their disassembly describes taxanes, which act in the M phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding tubulin to arrest metaphase describes vinca alkaloids, which act in the M phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cross-linking DNA independently of the cell cycle describes alkylating and platinum agents.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 4 pancreatic cancer. She has no significant medical history and is concerned about how her immune system became so weak. Her oncologist explains that the tumor secretes a cytokine in large quantities that broadly suppresses the activity of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant cytokine that some tumors secrete to downregulate multiple immune lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant capable of suppressing the activities of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, and that some tumor cells secrete it in large quantities to suppress the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a cell-surface protein that binds the Fas receptor on T cells to trigger apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells; it is not a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycocalyx is extracellular matrix material that masks surface antigens, not a cytokine that suppresses immune lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-2 promotes T cell proliferation and activation, the opposite of immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells rather than broadly suppressing immune cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms allows tumor cells to evade immune detection specifically by masking their surface antigens?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Antigen masking occurs when tumor cells coat themselves in excess extracellular matrix (glycocalyx).
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tumor cells secrete an excess of extracellular matrix material called glycocalyx. This thick coating masks the antigens on cancer cells, making it more difficult for immune cells to target them for destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Downregulating antigen expression is the outgrowth-of-antigen-variants mechanism, in which the antigen is lost rather than hidden.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of MHC class I removes the platform that displays antigen to cytotoxic T cells; it does not mask antigens with a coating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta secretion broadly suppresses immune cells and does not physically mask antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L1 upregulation engages the PD-1 checkpoint to inhibit T cells rather than masking antigens.

questions.stem: A tumor subclone continues to display abundant tumor antigen, yet cytotoxic CD8+ T cells can no longer recognize or kill it. Analysis shows the cells have acquired a mutation that eliminates a surface receptor normally present on all nucleated cells. Loss of which of the following molecules best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells identify targets via MHC class I; tumor loss of MHC class I prevents recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: MHC class I is a receptor present on all cells that displays antigens on the cell surface. Some tumor subclones undergo mutations that cause loss of MHC molecules so they are no longer recognized by cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 molecules are co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells; they are not present on all nucleated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a molecule tumor cells lose to escape recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Fas receptor is on T cells and mediates apoptosis when engaged by tumor FasL; losing it would not affect antigen recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells, not a molecule displayed on tumor cells for recognition.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced lung cancer that has failed multiple rounds of chemotherapy is started on pembrolizumab (Keytruda). Which of the following best describes how this medication helps the immune system attack the tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It engineers the patient's T cells to target CD19

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an antibody that binds PD-1 on T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neutralizes secreted TGF-beta in the tumor microenvironment

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restores MHC class I expression on tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies excess co-stimulatory signal directly to tumor cells

explanation.summary: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 antibody that blocks the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells upregulate PD-L1 and PD-L2, which activate the PD-1 receptor on T cells and suppress them. Keytruda is an antibody that binds the PD-1 receptor on T cells, preventing it from interacting with PD-L1 on cancer cells, giving the immune system a fighting chance to eliminate the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Engineering T cells to target CD19 describes CAR-T cell therapy, not a PD-1 antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutralizing TGF-beta is a different immunosuppression pathway and is not the mechanism of pembrolizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pembrolizumab does not alter MHC class I expression on tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug does not deliver co-stimulation to tumor cells; it removes an inhibitory checkpoint signal.

questions.stem: A tumor is found to upregulate an inhibitory receptor that binds the B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells and thereby reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor on T cells. Which of the following molecules is being upregulated?

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands, dampening T cell co-stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can upregulate the inhibitory receptor CTLA-4, which binds its ligands, the B7 molecules, from antigen-presenting cells and reduces the engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL binds the Fas receptor to induce T cell apoptosis and has no role in B7/CD28 competition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC class II presents antigen to helper T cells and is not an inhibitory receptor for B7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-L1 engages the PD-1 receptor on T cells; it does not bind B7 or block CD28.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine, not a receptor that competes for B7.

questions.stem: A melanoma expresses a cell-surface ligand that engages a death receptor on approaching cytotoxic T cells, causing those T cells to die via the extrinsic apoptosis pathway. Which of the following ligands is the tumor most likely expressing?

explanation.summary: Tumors such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which triggers extrinsic-pathway apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which binds the Fas receptor on T cells, leading to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7-1 is a co-stimulatory ligand that promotes T cell activation, not death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a tumor ligand that induces apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycocalyx is a physical coating that masks antigens and does not engage a death receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L2 engages PD-1 to inhibit T cells but does not directly trigger extrinsic-pathway apoptosis through a death receptor.

questions.stem: A T cell encounters a tumor cell that presents antigen through MHC but fails to deliver a co-stimulatory second signal. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes anergic or undergoes apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It differentiates into a memory T cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It proliferates into an activated effector clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes large amounts of TGF-beta

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates MHC class I on the tumor cell

explanation.summary: T cells require two signals; antigen without co-stimulation leads to anergy or apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A T cell can only be activated after receiving two signals: antigen recognition (Signal 1) and a co-stimulatory signal from the antigen-presenting cell (Signal 2). If the co-stimulatory signal is not received, the T cell becomes unresponsive (anergic) or undergoes apoptosis, which tumor cells exploit to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Memory differentiation follows productive activation, which does not occur without Signal 2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Effector proliferation requires both signals; without co-stimulation the T cell is not activated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is secreted by tumor cells, not by T cells lacking co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A T cell does not restore MHC class I on the tumor cell; MHC expression is a tumor property.

questions.stem: A patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma initially responds to CAR-T cell therapy engineered against CD19, but later relapses. Biopsy of the recurrent tumor shows the malignant B cells no longer express CD19. Which of the following best explains the relapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The engineered T cells lost their MHC class I molecules

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineered T cells were suppressed by CD28 co-stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tumor cells began secreting glycocalyx to physically block the CAR-T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor cells lost expression of the target antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor cells upregulated MHC class I to hide from the CAR-T cells

explanation.summary: Antigen escape occurs when tumor cells stop expressing the CAR-T target (CD19).
explanation.whyCorrect: In CAR-T therapy the patient's own T cells are engineered to target a specific antigen such as CD19 on B cells. A well-known challenge is that cancer cells may stop expressing CD19 on their surface, so there is no longer a target for the engineered T cells, allowing relapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CAR-T cells recognize CD19 directly and do not depend on tumor MHC; loss of the T cells' own MHC does not explain relapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 co-stimulation promotes, rather than suppresses, T cell activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The biopsy shows loss of CD19, not a glycocalyx coating, as the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CAR-T recognition of CD19 is MHC-independent, so upregulating MHC class I would not hide the tumor from CAR-T cells.

questions.stem: In a melanoma, highly immunogenic tumor subclones are eliminated by the host immune system, while other subclones that have lost or downregulated their surface antigens survive and expand. Which mechanism of immune evasion does this describe?

explanation.summary: Selective survival of antigen-negative subclones is the outgrowth of antigen variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a subclone is highly immunogenic it is eliminated, whereas some tumor subclones lose expression of a surface antigen or downregulate antigen expression so they are not recognized by immune cells. This has been observed in cancers such as melanoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen masking hides antigens under a glycocalyx coat; here the antigens are actually lost, not covered.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PD-L1 checkpoint engagement inhibits T cells directly and does not describe subclone selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TGF-beta immunosuppression is cytokine-mediated and does not involve selection of antigen-negative subclones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lack of co-stimulation causes T cell anergy/apoptosis and is distinct from loss of tumor antigen.

questions.stem: A medical student reads that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them, and that avoiding this process is one of the hallmarks of cancer. This normal protective function is best described by which of the following terms?

explanation.summary: Immune surveillance is the immune system's continuous scanning for and destruction of malignant cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term immune surveillance implies that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them; avoiding immune destruction is one of the hallmarks of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is an unresponsive state of T cells that lack co-stimulation, not immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen masking is a tumor evasion strategy, not a normal immune function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cachexia is the wasting syndrome associated with TNF-alpha in malignancy, unrelated to immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Checkpoint blockade is a therapy that uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1, not the normal scanning function.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced malignancy develops profound weight loss and muscle wasting. A cytokine elevated in this patient is known to cause cachexia in malignancy and to recruit white blood cells, and it is distinct from the immunosuppressive cytokine that tumors use to evade immunity. Which of the following cytokines is most likely responsible for the wasting?

explanation.summary: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and leads to white blood cell recruitment, distinguishing it from TGF-beta, the immunosuppressant tumors secrete to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a death-inducing surface ligand that triggers T cell apoptosis, not a cause of cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-2 activates and expands T cells and does not cause cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PD-L1 is a checkpoint ligand on tumor cells, not a cytokine that causes wasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is the immunosuppressive cytokine that downregulates immune lineages; it is not the cause of cachexia described here.

questions.stem: A newer class of cancer therapy, described as checkpoint blockade, uses antibodies to restore T cell function against tumors. Against which of the following pairs of targets are these checkpoint-blockade antibodies directed?

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I and MHC class II

explanation.summary: Checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function.
explanation.whyCorrect: New cancer therapy known as checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function; it is now approved for advanced-stage solid tumors and some forms of lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 and B7 are activating co-stimulatory molecules; blocking them would suppress, not restore, T cell function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas and FasL mediate apoptosis and are not the targets of approved checkpoint-blockade therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I and II present antigen and are not the targets of checkpoint-blockade antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta and TNF-alpha are cytokines and are not the checkpoint targets named for this therapy.
